title: Build, Not Buy: The Semiconductor Lesson that Indian AI Experts Must Learn
gist: Bhandari argues India's semiconductor mission quietly outperformed its far more glamorous AI mission because ISM built physical capacity (Micron Gujarat, Tata Assam packaging, the Tata-PSMC Dholera fab and its ASML MoU) while the India AI Mission mostly procured GPUs — 38,000 by late 2025 against a 10,000 target — on the untested assumption that global AI supply will stay freely available. He marshals the Biden AI Diffusion Framework, the GAO ruling that its rescission is not yet legally effective, and India's exclusion from Anthropic's restricted Claude Mythos Preview access list as evidence that assumption is breaking, and prescribes an ASML-style bet on advanced packaging and interposers — a segment U.S. export controls largely do not touch.

insights.claim: India's Semiconductor Mission, given the harder industrial task of physically siting global chip firms on Indian soil, has quietly outperformed the more glamorous India AI Mission by promising only chips, cleanrooms, and committed capital rather than moonshots.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: Industrial-policy credibility in India is currently concentrated in semis, not AI — a signal for where state capital and follow-on private capex will actually convert into assets.
insights.locator: When historians write about India’s technology decade

insights.claim: Micron's assembly and test facility in Gujarat and Tata Electronics' packaging plant in Assam are both close to transitioning to commercial-scale production, while LAM Research and Applied Materials have established tools presence in India.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: India's back-end semiconductor buildout is moving from announcement to revenue-stage output — a near-term inflection for OSAT and equipment supply chains.
insights.locator: Today, Micron’s assembly and test facility in Gujarat

insights.claim: The Tata-PSMC fab in Dholera, India's first commercial mega-fab, has signed an MoU with ASML and is seeking to deploy ASML lithography equipment, placing India on the short list of countries the Dutch firm trusts with its machines.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: ASML tool placement is a hard third-party validation of a national chip ecosystem — far more informative than subsidy announcements about who actually gets to fabricate.
insights.locator: The Tata-PSMC fab in Dholera

insights.claim: The Tata-ASML MoU signals that India's semiconductor ecosystem is attracting participants who anticipate demand rather than merely follow it, a qualitative change in the type of counterparty engaging with India.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: Watch which suppliers commit ahead of Indian demand — forward-leaning entrants are the leading indicator that an ecosystem has crossed a credibility threshold.
insights.locator: The Tata-ASML MoU also signals something far more consequential

insights.claim: The India AI Mission was approved in March 2024 with a ₹10,372 crore budget of which roughly ₹4,568 crore was earmarked for compute capacity, and it assembled around 38,000 GPUs by late 2025 against an initial goal of 10,000.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: The GPU target was beaten nearly fourfold, so any shortfall in Indian AI capability is not a compute-quantity problem — it is a value-chain-position problem.
insights.locator: Compare this to the India AI Mission (IAM)

insights.claim: Acquiring GPUs is not the same as building an AI future, and compute purchased is not the same as capability built.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: The core distinction for judging any sovereign-AI program: count owned capability, not installed accelerators.
insights.quote: compute purchased is not the same as capability built
insights.locator: Though the IAM brought compute to India

insights.claim: The India Semiconductor Mission assembled a small team of industry experts and delivered across almost the entire value chain without producing working papers or concept notes, in contrast to India's AI effort.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: Volume of published strategy documents is inversely correlated with delivery here — a usable heuristic for reading government tech missions.
insights.quote: It simply delivered, across almost all parts of the value chain.
insights.locator: The ISM put together a small team of industry experts

insights.claim: Across five Indian government AI white papers issued between January 2025 and March 2026 — on AI governance guidelines, AI governance, democratizing AI infrastructure access, a techno-legal governance approach, and indigenous foundational models — compute is mentioned only as something to be procured, never built or manufactured.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: The procurement framing is baked into Indian AI doctrine at the document level, which means the policy gap is conceptual and will not close by adding budget.
insights.quote: compute is only mentioned as something to be procured, not built or manufactured

themes.theme: The unexamined assumption of open AI supply

insights.claim: India's AI strategy rests on an unexamined assumption that access to the global AI supply chain is and will remain freely available — that India can procure compute abroad, run models trained elsewhere, and layer Indian applications on top indefinitely.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: The single largest unhedged risk in India's AI buildout is counterparty access, not capital or talent.
insights.quote: embedded in India’s AI strategy is an assumption so comfortable it has rarely been interrogated
insights.locator: The Assumption Nobody Examined

insights.claim: The Indian government has formally stated it is pursuing an 'AI diffusion' strategy of deploying AI applications across sectors, reflecting a debate that has mostly settled in favor of the application layer over underlying AI technology.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: India has effectively declared its position in the AI stack — investors should ask what happens to that position if upstream access tightens.
insights.locator: A formal press release from the Indian government

insights.claim: The Biden administration's January 2025 Framework for AI Diffusion imposed cumulative AI-chip import caps on all but eighteen exempt countries, which qualified because they held most global AI data center capacity and were Five Eyes members, close NATO allies, or existing semiconductor hubs — a list India was not on.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: The exemption criteria were structural, not negotiable — India cannot lobby its way into a tier it does not structurally qualify for.
insights.locator: First, under the Joe Biden administration’s January 2025 Framework

insights.claim: Reaching higher chip-import thresholds under the AI Diffusion Framework required government-to-government assurances demanding diplomatic, capital, and regulatory capacity that India is still building.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: State capacity, not chip supply, is the binding constraint on India's access under any tiered export-control regime.
insights.locator: Reaching higher thresholds under this now-rescinded framework

insights.claim: The U.S. Government Accountability Office has ruled that the AI Diffusion Rule cannot be considered formally rescinded because the rescission announcement is itself a rule under the Congressional Review Act, so it must be submitted to Congress and the Comptroller General before taking effect.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: The chip-diffusion regime is legally live, not dead — a latent re-imposition risk for every non-exempt buyer of AI accelerators.
insights.locator: Indeed, recently, the United States Government Accountability Office

themes.theme: Frontier-model access as an export-control frontier

insights.claim: Anthropic restricted access to its April 2026 Claude Mythos Preview model to roughly forty entities globally because of its cybersecurity capabilities, and thirty-nine of those were American with the sole exception being the United Kingdom's AI Safety Institute — India was excluded.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: Frontier-model access is now allocated on institutional trust, not market size — a hard constraint on any national AI plan built on foreign models.
insights.locator: Second, when Anthropic announced its Claude Mythos Preview model

insights.claim: The U.S. government ordered Anthropic to suspend access to its Fable 5 model for all foreign nationals including its own employees, a step outside usual Department of Commerce guidance that raised questions about the predictability of an export-control regime that had until then targeted only advanced AI chips.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: Export controls have crossed from hardware into model weights and even employee access — repricing the durability of any foreign firm's dependence on U.S. frontier models.
insights.locator: Subsequently, the U.S. government ordered Anthropic

insights.claim: India's large market size does not buy preferential access to frontier AI models because it has not built the safety institutes, evaluation and testing frameworks, and enterprise-grade security infrastructure that earn early access.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: Building evaluation and security institutions is a cheaper, faster lever on frontier access than compute spending — and India is not pulling it.
insights.locator: This has been a wake-up call to those who perhaps thought

insights.claim: Even at the application layer, Indian developers cannot assume model access will remain available or fair, because large AI companies can bundle models into their own apps or partner with telecom operators to package AI access with cloud storage, security tools, and GPU access.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: Vertical bundling by model providers is the mechanism that could squeeze independent application-layer margins — the exact layer India has chosen to occupy.
insights.locator: Even at the application layer, Indian developers

themes.theme: Why 'DPI for AI' fails on imported compute

insights.claim: The digital-public-infrastructure-for-AI approach is impractical if the underlying compute is procured rather than built, because its core promise is reducing prohibitive costs for smaller players.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: India's flagship access-democratization model breaks down at the hardware cost layer — governance design cannot fix an imported cost base.
insights.quote: Its value lies in creating predictable, transparent and interoperable access pathways, particularly for smaller firms, research institutions, and startups that face prohibitive entry barriers.
insights.locator: Lastly, even the “DPI [digital public infrastructure] for AI” approach

insights.claim: Importing GPUs at global market prices that may be tariff-laden, export-control-limited, or inflated by demand surges from U.S. hyperscalers keeps India's underlying compute cost stubbornly high regardless of how the access layer is designed.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: Indian AI compute pricing is a residual of hyperscaler demand and U.S. trade policy — a direct read-through from Western capex cycles to Indian startup unit economics.
insights.locator: However, if India is importing GPUs at global market prices

insights.claim: A well-designed access layer built on expensive imported hardware is like subsidizing bus service on an expensive toll road: the governance is democratic but the underlying economics stay market-driven and are not inherently inclusive.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: A transferable test for any 'democratized access' infrastructure claim: check whether the subsidy touches the cost base or only the interface.
insights.quote: A well-designed access layer on top of expensive imported hardware is like subsidizing bus service on an expensive toll road
insights.locator: A well-designed access layer on top of expensive imported hardware

insights.claim: In the 1990s ASML was a distant third behind Nikon and Canon, smaller, less capitalized, and dependent on Zeiss for lenses it could not manufacture itself, making EUV look too expensive and speculative to displace incumbents.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: The dominant chokepoint of the modern chip supply chain started as the least likely bidder — evidence that entrenched market share is a weak predictor of terminal position in deep-tech.
insights.locator: In the 1990s, ASML was a distant third

insights.claim: ASML reached its position by co-designing DUV lenses with Zeiss, forming the EUV Euclides consortium in 1998 to pull in European partners and governments, and then partnering with Intel, which backed multiple lithography suppliers precisely to avoid single-vendor dependence.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: Customer fear of single-vendor dependence is a reliable funding source for challengers — the same opening exists today for anyone attacking incumbent AI hardware.
insights.locator: ASML did not reach that conclusion

insights.claim: ASML is today the sole global producer of EUV machines, works with over 5,000 suppliers, and has become one of the most critical chokepoints in the entire global technology order.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: Quantifies the prize for winning a deep-tech chokepoint: monopoly plus a 5,000-supplier ecosystem plus geopolitical leverage.
insights.locator: Today, ASML is the sole producer of EUV machines

insights.claim: The transferable lesson from ASML is the nature of the bet: identify a technically daunting problem the market needs solved, build coalitions rather than going it alone, and make yourself indispensable to those who might have dismissed you.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: A concrete template for evaluating national or corporate deep-tech strategy: does the bet target indispensability, or just participation?
insights.quote: It identified a technically daunting problem that the market needed solved, built coalitions rather than doing it alone, and made itself indispensable to the people who might have dismissed it.
insights.locator: The lesson is not that India should try to become ASML

themes.theme: Advanced packaging as India's export-control-free lane

insights.claim: India's tradition of building technology for development rather than leverage — shared space imagery, exported DPI, vaccine diplomacy, generic pharmaceuticals — is admirable but insufficient as a framework for building AI infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: Argues India's proven export model does not transfer to AI, implying a strategic doctrine change is required before capital allocation changes.
insights.locator: India has a tradition of building technology for development

insights.claim: India should ask what sits at the intersection of what the world needs, what India can build, and what the future will reward, rather than prematurely fixing its role in the AI value chain at the application layer.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: A three-way screen for national deep-tech bets that argues against the current consensus that India's slot is applications.
insights.locator: India must ask what is at the intersection

insights.claim: AI hardware startups historically failed because developers would not rewrite software for new architectures, but building AI chips compatible with CUDA-heavy environments has lowered enterprise and developer switching costs.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: CUDA compatibility is the entry ticket for challenger silicon — a concrete screen for which AI-chip startups have a real adoption path.
insights.locator: Many AI hardware startups have struggled in the past

insights.claim: NITI Aayog's semiconductor roadmap identifies advanced packaging as a key focus area where India should secure self-reliance for domestic demand while aggressively targeting a top-three global position.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: An explicit official target in the one chip segment where India has structural room — the clearest published signal of where Indian semi policy money goes next.
insights.quote: India should aim to secure self-reliance for domestic demand while aggressively targeting a top-three global position.
insights.locator: Advanced Packaging

insights.claim: Advanced packaging moved from an upstream afterthought to essential AI infrastructure because generative AI exposed the limits of single-chip architectures and LLM proliferation surged memory-bandwidth demand, creating HBM that traditional packaging cannot produce.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: Explains the structural, not cyclical, driver behind HBM and advanced-packaging demand — the bottleneck persists as long as LLM scaling does.
insights.locator: Packaging was earlier seen as a largely upstream part

insights.claim: Stacking many small chips vertically shortens inter-chip distance, lowering latency and delivering a significant performance jump without upgrading to the next-generation process node.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: Packaging is a substitute for node shrinks, which decouples AI performance gains from leading-edge lithography access — the crux of why it is India's opening.
insights.locator: Compressed stacks of chips means that there is shorter distance

insights.claim: Most U.S. export controls apply to advanced downstream elements such as semiconductor manufacturing equipment, EDA tools, and advanced AI chips, which leaves advanced packaging comparatively unhindered and therefore easier for countries like India to enter.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: Export-control geography defines where non-aligned states can build real chip capability — packaging is the open lane, and capital should follow the regulatory gap.
insights.locator: Indeed, most U.S. export controls are applicable

insights.claim: India could target interposers — the devices connecting chips to each other and to the wafer substrate — because they require only foundry-grade 65 nm process nodes, infrastructure India can readily build.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: A specific, capital-feasible entry point: 65 nm interposer capacity, not leading-edge fabs, is where Indian chip capex earns a defensible position.
insights.locator: Here, India could focus on interposers

insights.claim: Stacked multi-material chip layers generate significant heat requiring thermal management, and where traditional air cooling fails, techniques such as liquid cooling can be explored.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: Thermal management is an adjacent, less-contested niche that scales directly with advanced packaging adoption.
insights.locator: Consequently, the various layers of different materials

themes.theme: Unknown unknowns and where advantage is built

insights.claim: India's AI strategy has been organized almost entirely around 'known knowns' like GPUs and governance frameworks, has only begun engaging 'known unknowns' like sovereign models and frontier-AI evaluation infrastructure, and has not touched the third Rumsfeld category where strategic advantage is most often built.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: Reframes the AI-capability gap as a question-selection failure rather than a resource failure — useful for auditing any national or corporate tech roadmap.
insights.locator: The “Unknown Unknowns” We Have Not Asked

insights.claim: The strategic question India should be asking is whether there is a component, material, process, or infrastructure layer in the AI stack that current AI powers will need in quantities and at a scale they cannot yet imagine.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: Points at the highest-return search space in AI supply chains: latent physical bottlenecks that scaling will expose but nobody has yet provisioned.
insights.quote: Is there something in the AI tech stack—a component, material, process, layer of infrastructure—that the current AI powers will need in quantities they do not yet have, at a scale they cannot yet imagine?
insights.locator: But the third category, the things that India has not even thought

insights.claim: ISM progress on packaging, fabrication, and tooling proves that patient, specific industrial policy can work in India, matching its demonstrated ability to execute hard technical problems in space, pharmaceuticals, and DPI.
insights.speaker: Konark Bhandari
insights.so_what: Grounds the bull case for Indian deep-tech execution in a track record rather than aspiration — the differentiator is specificity of mandate.
insights.locator: This is not naïveté
